frames.narration: An illustration with invented numbers. Ana and Ben open the same design. The multiplayer server for this file holds it in memory at sequence number 100, and each browser downloads a copy.

Ana drags the rectangle to x 40 and sets its fill to red, then to green. At the same moment Ben sets the fill to blue. Each browser shows its own change immediately and remembers which of its edits are not yet confirmed.

The changes reach the server in some order: Ana's red, Ben's blue, Ana's x, Ana's green. The server gives each a sequence number and keeps the latest value of each property. The fill ends up green, and x is 40, because the two properties do not conflict. No clock is needed: arrival order decides.

The server tells everyone, in order. Ana's browser skips #101 (her own red) and #102 (Ben's blue) because her green is still unconfirmed, so her screen never flickers back to red or blue. Ben's browser skips #101 until his own blue is confirmed in #102. After #104 both screens show x 40 and a green fill.
A moment later the server writes the new changes to the journal as one batched entry covering sequence numbers 101 to 104. It writes asynchronously, so editing does not wait for the journal.

Much less often the server writes a checkpoint: the whole file, tagged with the sequence number it reflects. The latest checkpoint here was written at #100, before these edits, and the next one is not due yet.

The server process crashes before the next checkpoint. A new process takes ownership of the file, loads the checkpoint at #100, asks the journal for entries after it, and replays #101 to #104. The file is back at its latest state, with nothing lost that reached the journal.
